source.title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
source.authors: Le-Qun Wang; Jiang-Wei Pan; Feng-Di Che; L. Baltrunas

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether model-size scaling trends transfer to an industrial homepage-recommendation setting, rather than testing language-model scaling in the original setting.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the model-size sweep in Figure 3, which reports pretraining and WBC losses. The context-enrichment sweep changes prompt information, not training-token count, and does not test a listed version; the paper's online engagement and RL-diversity results are not scale-dependent results.
record.test_reason: A model-size sweep (∼120M–∼900M) of a decoder-only transformer trained on tokenized Netflix homepage data. It reports pretraining next-token loss and WBC post-training loss on a held-out set, and the authors describe both as falling in a power-law-like way. This is a new, non-text setting bearing on V5. It is not language-model text pretraining, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say both pretraining and WBC losses decrease power-law-like with model size, 'mirroring' LLM scaling, so capacity scaling helps. However, the effect is small: about 1.3% WBC loss over 120M–900M, versus about 6.9% from context enrichment. They conclude that in their regime prompt enrichment matters more than capacity, at least until the context is saturated.
record.recipe_differences: Measures loss scaling in a domain-specific generative recommender, including WBC post-training, rather than language-model scaling in the original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that context enrichment changes WBC loss substantially, but this is a separate sweep and is not a fitting-choice comparison within the model-size scaling experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed ∼200M size, enriching the user context cut WBC loss by about 6.9% cumulatively. Scaling from 120M to 900M cut it by about 1.3%. Several single context additions beat the whole 7.5× capacity scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommender transformers, gains from richer input information or representation can exceed gains from parameter scaling until the context saturates.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems
record.problems: The model-size sweep covers only roughly an order of magnitude. Figure 3 values and uncertainty for the scaling results are not recoverable from the supplied text. The paper says individual ablations span different configurations and data snapshots, so it reports relative comparisons within each study.

untested.parts: Other modalities (image, video), repeated-data regimes and transfer are not tested. Scaling in data or compute is not tested, only parameters. The range spans under one order of magnitude (∼7.5×) with four points, so 'several orders of magnitude' is not tested. No power-law fit or exponent is reported.

missing.what: Quantitative WBC loss reduction from model scaling: about 1.3% from 120M to 900M. This is the only numeric magnitude for the scaling sweep.

record.verdict_notes: The sweep is a minor component of a systems paper. No exponent, fit or error bars are given. The authors also say ablations used different configurations and data snapshots. The reader's limits_scope label was dropped because the narrow range and single domain are untested parts of V5, not shown qualifications. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The model is a homepage recommender, not a language model; the study does not test language-model held-out loss against parameters, training tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions for substantially larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or optimal parameter/token split is tested.
Depth, width, and other architecture choices are not compared at fixed parameter count.

Only a Netflix homepage recommendation setting is tested, over a model-size range of approximately 120M to 900M parameters. Other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The study does not test whether downstream-task performance scales predictably with model size or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits under different counting, scheduling, data, or fitting choices is reported.

rows.subject: GenPage
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and measured next-token-prediction loss.
rows.note: The authors state that the loss decreases in a power-law-like fashion. Exact values cannot be assigned from the supplied figure text; the sweep spans roughly an order of magnitude in parameters.
rows.check: The state should be observed, not partial: the authors state the loss decreases 'in a power-law-like fashion' across all four sizes (120M, 200M, 450M, 900M). There is no fitted exponent or uncertainty. The value can only be read roughly from the Figure 3 axis, about 2.52 to 2.38. The narrow range is an untested part of V5, not a reason for partial.

rows.subject: GenPage
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and measured weighted binary cross-entropy loss.
rows.note: The authors state that the loss decreases in a power-law-like fashion. Exact values cannot be assigned from the supplied figure text; the sweep spans roughly an order of magnitude in parameters.
rows.check: The value should not be 'figure only'. Section 7.3 states that scaling from 120M to 900M 'reduces WBC loss by roughly 1.3%' (Figure 3 axis about 0.326 to 0.322). The state should be observed on the authors' power-law-like description. The baseline is the 120M model.

relationships.condition: GenPage homepage recommender, ∼120M–∼900M parameters, pretraining next-token loss and WBC post-training loss on held-out data
relationships.reason: Both losses fall monotonically with model size; the authors call this power-law-like (R1, R2; WBC about −1.3%). This rests on author description and the figure, with no fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: Both held-out losses decrease monotonically with size, including about a 1.3% WBC loss reduction, but the reported power-law-like trend has no fitted law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GenPage pretraining and WBC post-training in the Netflix homepage recommendation setting
reader_labels.reason: Both losses decrease in a power-law-like fashion as model size increases in this setting (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The evidence covers only approximately 120M–900M parameters and reports power-law-like behavior, not a test across several orders of magnitude or across other modalities and regimes (R1, R2).
